proposed_edges.relationship: Portelli uses Gramsci’s organic-intellectual concept to explain intellectual responsibility as learning from popular worlds and carrying their voices into public discourse.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own interview with Paulo Álvarez Bravo in Santiago, 4 December 2015, published 2017. Portelli invokes Gramsci but separately credits mentor Gianni Bosio’s inverted intellectual and the agency of narrators; neither Bosio nor those narrators are replaced by a generic Gramscian lineage. This is a specified conceptual use, not a claim that Gramsci founded oral history. The interview prints Bossio; the established Gianni Bosio identity is retained. Gramsci’s original text was not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Sangster explicitly takes Portelli as a guide for interpreting what working people wanted, believed and later made of their experiences, alongside the events themselves.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sangster’s own 2013 account links this resource to attention to subjectivity and the interview relationship. She also rejects an overly simple progression from naive recovery to sophisticated interpretation; this is not a claim that meaning replaces evidence or that Portelli supplied every element of her approach. The article’s body misspells his given name as Alexandro, but n 27 identifies Alessandro Portelli’s 1991 essay and p 50. The 2014 reader version and the 2013 journal article are distinct; the proposed witness is the actual journal PDF.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Malena reproduces Portelli’s recollection, Ginzburg criticized his early Terni manuscript for explanations that reduced the richness of the narrators’ stories; Portelli thought the criticism right.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Adelisa Malena’s 2016 essay,p 176 and n 54, follows Alessandro Casellato’s 2014 discussion and reproduces Portelli’s 1987 recollection. Cesare Bermani and Liliana Lanzardo retain their roles in that original conversation. Neither the 1987 original nor Ginzburg’s manuscript comments were freshly read. This is a particular editorial/methodological criticism, not rejection of oral history or evidence that all Portelli’s practice descends from microhistory. A separate 2022 own interview confirms the Ginzburg/Microstorie connection without independently reproducing this criticism.

proposed_edges.relationship: Cronon presents Crosby’s studies of migrating organisms and introduced pathogens as practical lessons of environmental history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cronon’s own 1993 presidential address, pp. 8 and 10, explicitly footnotes these lessons to The Columbian Exchange (1972) and Ecological Imperialism (1986). This is a specified use in explaining the field’s practical value, not evidence that every part of Cronon’s method comes from Crosby. Cronon also insists on particular places and times and on the limits of general environmental lessons. Both cited Crosby books remain unread in full. Note 16 is on printed p. 21; note 25 is on p. 22. This fresh check corrects the inherited collective locator placing both notes on p. 22 without replacing the old source record.

proposed_edges.relationship: Worster uses Crosby’s ecological-imperialism concept in the Kentucky bluegrass example; Crosby separately endorses Worster’s agroecological research agenda.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Two distinct intellectual actions in the same 1990 round table are retained in one directed contribution record. Fresh selected English primary transcription of Worster’s 1990 essay, pp. 1087–1089, particularly p. 1088 and n. 4. Worster names the concept and its source, while warning that the bluegrass example is more complicated than simple environmental determinism. This is a specific conceptual resource in his argument, not a claim that Crosby originated all of Worster’s environmental history. The English page images were not available; the witness is a page-labelled transcription. The original source’s earlier Portuguese-translation and 1993-reprint reading scopes remain distinct. Crosby’s own response to Transformations of the Earth, first page (1107), says that the essay continues their agreement and argues that agroecosystems deserve greater historical attention. He contrasts agriculture’s long history with the industrial revolution and discusses soil, water and simplified biota. This is a documented response and endorsement, distinct from Worster’s use of Crosby’s ecological-imperialism concept. Only the publisher’s first-page facsimile was read; pp. 1108–1110 and Worster’s later reply remain unread. No claim of complete agreement across those unread pages or the entire round table is made.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his 2004 preface Crosby identifies Pomeranz’s Great Divergence as the clearest exposition of the new scenario linking European industrialization to overseas ecological resources.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Crosby’s own second-edition preface, pp. xv–xx, explicitly names Pomeranz at p. xvii, n. 1, then develops the scenario through overseas ecosystems, resources and labour, and says that he is proud to have contributed to it. This later self-positioning is dated 2004 and is not projected into the original 1986 book. The direction records Pomeranz as an acknowledged resource for this later framing, not priority for Crosby’s original ecological-imperialism argument or proof that Pomeranz supplied every assertion in the preface. Pomeranz’s whole book and Crosby’s chapters 2–12 remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pagden uses Pocock’s account of political languages as distinguishable language-games to explain how historians reconstruct an argument’s vocabularies, conventions and intelligibility.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pagden’s own opening discussion explicitly names and uses Pocock’s formulation. The publisher’s substantive opening excerpt was read; the complete 1987 introduction and Pocock’s chapter were not freshly read. This is a particular methodological resource, not influence inferred from the editorship or the whole Cambridge school. The print contribution is 1987; 2009 is the online publication date.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. The witness is not backdated to 1971, and the date of each introductory revision is not independently established. Todorov’s original book and the complete letters remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Armitage credits Pagden with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral study that developed into The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Armitage’s own acknowledgments p. x explicitly group Pagden with Chris Bayly, Peter Burke, Patrick Collinson and Istvan Hont in this Cambridge phase. All retain credit. This supports the named research contribution, not sole supervision, a particular question whose wording is unknown, or an inference from first meeting or institutional membership. Selected acknowledgments and publication leaves were read; Armitage’s full monograph remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thomas’s review identifies Taylor as a specific target of Pagden’s defense of Enlightenment cosmopolitanism against communitarian restrictions on moral judgment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Keith Thomas’s 2014 review of The Enlightenment: And Why It Still Matters (2013), in the paragraphs on communitarian adversaries. The localist and moral-relativist characterization is Pagden’s position as reported by Thomas, not an editorial judgment that it accurately exhausts Taylor’s philosophy. Alasdair MacIntyre retains co-target credit; no response by Taylor is inferred. Pagden’s original book and Taylor’s underlying works were not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: A comparison of the positions juxtaposed in The New Imperial Histories Reader contrasts Pagden’s rejection of an American-empire label with Chatterjee’s argument that the new global order is imperial.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: An editorial teaching comparison grounded in Barbara Bush’s 2010 substantive review, which explicitly identifies these opposed positions in the reader’s final section. Stephen Howe is the reader’s editor. The comparison is undirected: it does not assert a personal reply, direct encounter, influence, or agreement across every definition of empire. The two original contributions and the complete reader were not freshly read; the positions remain attributed to Bush’s account of their juxtaposition.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost uses Bloch to argue that historical facts depend on questions rather than emerging from a preliminary collection of documents.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Specific methodological resource, not a personal apprenticeship or wholesale Annales lineage. Prost also preserves the value of the methodological school’s critical rules. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost endorses Febvre’s insistence that historians formulate problems and hypotheses before directing their inquiry.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The praise is explicitly attached to this methodological point; Prost’s introductory reservations about historians’ avoidance of philosophy are not erased. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost uses Weber’s counterfactual reasoning to identify and weigh historical causes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A specified argumentative resource, with Raymond Aron separately credited in the passage. Max Weber is not Eugen Weber; no personal contact is claimed. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost adopts Koselleck’s distinction between experience and expectation to reconstruct the open futures of past actors.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A concrete temporal distinction used against retrospective inevitability, not a claim that every aspect of Prost’s historical time comes from Koselleck. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost draws on Ricœur to connect probabilistic causal explanation with respect for historical uncertainty and freedom.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ricœur’s passage itself credits Raymond Aron; retain both levels of attribution, not an exclusive origin or an unqualified endorsement of all Ricœur’s philosophy. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost uses Bourdieu’s account of contested classifications to argue that social classes require historical reconstruction.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: A specified use within the criticism of ready-made social categories; Prost credits Bourdieu and his school, without treating Bourdieu as the sole source of the argument. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost follows de Certeau’s analysis of quotation as a device that gives historical writing authority and an effect of reality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Explicitly acknowledged analytical use; it coexists with Prost’s particular correction of the treatment of another’s words as a threat. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost uses White’s analysis of historical styles and prefiguration to illuminate the assumptions behind emplotment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Qualified intellectual use, explicitly compatible with a separate criticism of excessive formalism. Prost treats the typologies as flexible tendencies, not rigid correspondences. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: While finding White illuminating, Prost judges his formalism too systematic to be fully convincing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Narrow objection to formal systematization, not wholesale rejection of narrative theory. Do not attribute the following broader history/fiction discussion or every claim made about Veyne exclusively to White. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost criticizes the Labroussian paradigm’s ready-made classes, explanatory reductions and restricted room for agency.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The argument also recognizes its economic explanatory gains and says the agency problem is not exclusive to Labrousse or Marxist historians. It defends historically reconstructed classes, rather than abandoning social history. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Prost counters de Certeau’s account of the cited other as a threat by allowing respectful quotation to offer companionship and confirmation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Particular methodological correction within explicit substantial use of de Certeau; not a general dispute over archives or a claim that the risk of appropriation disappears. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Using Braudel’s remarks as reported by Dosse, Prost criticizes the marginal place that determinist social history leaves for human agency.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Specifically attributed criticism of the determinist rhetoric quoted in this passage, not a general rejection of Braudel. Prost explicitly says the problem extends beyond Labrousse and Marxist historians. Dosse is the named mediator; Braudel’s underlying statements and Dosse’s complete work were not freshly read. Prost’s separate use of Braudel’s warning about retrospective hindsight does not erase this objection. Selected authorial passage in the expanded digital edition, identified by EPUB ISBN 9782757843765 (BAnQ catalog: April 2014). Read through a public third-party transcription, not a collated print facsimile. No claim that the exact wording was present in 1996; complete book and cited originals unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Teaching overlap: Prost and Winter explicitly share a contextual, cross-national and cross-theme approach to the historiography of the Great War.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Editorial undirected comparison grounded in their joint methodological argument, not coauthorship alone or a claim that either caused the other’s approach. Their introduction identifies public and professional contexts, rejects narrow thematic/national boundaries and expressly accepts mutual responsibility for two voices. Selected English second-edition introduction 2020 read; French 2004 and English 2005 originals and complete 2020 book unread. The introduction also states exclusions and the need for wider coverage; no exhaustive global scope is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton identifies Spivak’s feminist critique of archival recovery in “The Rani of Sirmur” as a formative resource for her account of feminism and imperial history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burton’s own 2011 retrospective recalls reading the 1985 Rani essay as a graduate student and explains its challenge to universal historical recovery and liberal imperial feminism. Do not silently substitute the later “Can the Subaltern Speak?” essay for this encounter, infer personal mentorship, or treat Burton’s retrospective as a complete restatement of Spivak’s position. Selected retrospective pages read; the complete original Spivak essay was not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton credits Said’s Orientalism with major importance for her intellectual and political formation while retaining her feminist criticism of its treatment of gender.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This is Burton’s explicit assessment, not shared postcolonial vocabulary. She recalls reading Orientalism the year before the 1985 Rani encounter. The positive debt coexists with the separate gender criticism; it does not endorse Said’s entire argument. Selected retrospective read; Said’s original book was not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton criticizes Said’s inadequate engagement with women, gender and feminist analysis while explicitly acknowledging Orientalism’s importance to her own formation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This is Burton’s particular feminist criticism in her own retrospective, not rejection of Orientalism wholesale. She contrasts Spivak’s feminist starting point with this limit. Selected primary retrospective read; no original Said-body reading or reply by Said is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton uses Stuart Hall’s conjunctural framework to interpret domestic imperial culture as a historically contingent problem space requiring strategic intervention.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her p. 6 explicitly names Hall and defines the framework before applying it to her own trajectory. This supports a particular conceptual use, not personal mentorship inferred from Hazel Carby’s Birmingham connection. Footnote 9’s original source is outside the preview and has not been independently read; no independent quotation-authentication of Hall is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton uses Scott’s critique of the evidence of experience and her account of gender as an effect of power to explain her own situated interpretation of empire.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The retrospective explicitly attributes the experience critique to Scott on p. 10, then borrows Scott’s produced-gender analysis on p. 14. Burton refuses a view of her own position as transparent or fully knowable. Her subsequent account of performativity also credits Judith Butler and Bernard Cohn; it is not Scott’s sole creation. No personal mentoring or full original Scott-body reading is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton identifies Catherine Hall’s feminist remapping of home and empire as consequential to her imperial-history project, including the gendered imperial setting of political reform and Civilizing Subjects.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burton explicitly connects Hall’s critique of public/private separation with home/empire and discusses work done partly with Keith McClelland and Jane Rendall, whose credit is retained. Civilizing Subjects is Hall’s separate monograph. This is Burton’s own methodological evaluation and resource statement, not cofield influence or sole authorship of collaborative work. Original Hall books were not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton says that refracting gender-and-power insights through Butler’s work helped her understand nation and empire as performatively produced.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The same sentence gives Bernard Cohn’s anthropological history equal, distinct credit, with his durbar example; Cohn has no current endpoint and is recorded as a hold. The claim is a joint intellectual resource acknowledged by Burton, not sole Butler authorship of her entire method or a personal collaboration. Original Butler and Cohn works were not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton draws on Stoler’s emphasis on colonial regimes’ precarious vulnerability when explaining why imperial culture should not be treated as an irresistible juggernaut.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Burton explicitly pairs Stoler’s formulation with John Darwin’s chaotic pluralism as interpretive postures making room for agency and resistance while retaining empire’s coercive power. Darwin’s co-credit is preserved; he has no current endpoint. This is a bounded conceptual use, not general agreement with every Stoler argument, personal mentoring, or a body-reading claim for Along the Archival Grain.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton explicitly borrows Gilroy’s formulation of interdependent modalities to describe how race, gender and class structured lived imperial Englishness.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This is a particular, expressly acknowledged conceptual borrowing in Burton’s discussion of Catherine Hall and feminist history, not a general assertion that all her work derives from Gilroy or a personal relationship. The original Gilroy text behind note 30 is outside the preview and was not freshly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Burton criticizes Ornamentalism’s novelty claim and its failure to sustain an analysis of metropole–colony interdependence, arguing that it misreads Sinha’s and Catherine Hall’s accounts of empire’s constitutive role in domestic Britain.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Specific criticism in Burton’s own 2002 opening, reproduced as substantive authorial prose under Abstract on a third-party bibliographic page. She acknowledges Cannadine’s citations and declared interconnected model before criticizing its analytical limits. Sinha and Catherine Hall retain their distinct intellectual credit; neither is presented as a coauthor of Burton’s critique. The reproduced opening was freshly read, but the full article, original journal facsimile, Cannadine’s book and the original works of Sinha/Hall were not freshly read. No claim about the article’s unseen conclusion, a personal reply by Cannadine, or a complete rejection of every part of his work.
